questions.stem: An IV graph that is a straight line through the origin shows:

options.text: a resistance that grows with voltage
options.explanation: A growing resistance would bend the line, not keep it straight.
The straight proportional line is the signature of unchanging resistance.
Reverse bias shows a flat zero region, not a rising straight line.
A rising line records current growing with voltage.

questions.stem: Which component gives a linear IV graph at constant temperature?

options.explanation: The lamp's graph bends as its filament heats.
The diode's graph is strongly non-linear.
At steady temperature a fixed resistor's straight line passes through the origin.
An LDR's resistance moves with the light level.

questions.stem: On a non-linear IV graph, the resistance:

options.explanation: Constancy is the straight-line signature, not the curved one.
The curvature exists precisely because the resistance varies.
A zero resistance would be a vertical line, not a curve.

options.text: cannot be found at any point
options.explanation: Reading voltage and current at a point still gives the resistance there.

questions.stem: For a wire at steady temperature, doubling the voltage across it:

options.explanation: Direct proportionality: twice the push, twice the flow.
That falloff belongs to heating components like filament lamps.
Voltage is what drives the current through the wire.
That acceleration belongs to a forward-biased diode, not a wire.

questions.stem: Which statement about the resistance of a wire at constant temperature is true?

options.explanation: Rising resistance with current is the filament's behaviour, not a cool wire's.

options.text: it falls as the voltage rises
options.explanation: Nothing in a steady-temperature wire lowers its resistance.

options.text: it depends on the voltmeter used
options.explanation: The resistance belongs to the wire, not the meter.

options.text: it stays constant as the voltage varies
options.explanation: A steady-temperature wire keeps one resistance across the voltage range.

questions.stem: What shape does the IV graph of a fixed resistor take, and what does the shape tell you?
questions.modelAnswer: A straight line through the origin — the current is directly proportional to the voltage, so the resistance stays constant.

questions.stem: Name two components with non-linear IV graphs.
questions.modelAnswer: Filament lamps and diodes — thermistors and LDRs are non-linear too.

questions.stem: Explain what an IV graph running straight through the origin tells you about how the current behaves.
questions.modelAnswer: Current and voltage grow in step, so doubling one doubles the other — the current is directly proportional to the voltage and the resistance never changes.

questions.stem: A fixed resistor's IV graph passes through (2 V, 0.4 A) as a straight line through the origin. Predict the current at 5 V, then the resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: The line's steepness sets the ratio: current per volt = 0.4 ÷ 2 = 0.2 A per volt, so 5 V gives 5 × 0.2 = 1 A. The resistance is 2 ÷ 0.4 = 5 Ω.

questions.stem: As the voltage across a filament lamp increases, the current:

options.text: increases at a proportionally slower rate
options.explanation: The growing resistance bends the graph, so the current gains less and less.

options.text: increases at a proportionally faster rate
options.explanation: The lamp's rising resistance restrains the current instead.
Proportionality is the cool fixed resistor's behaviour.
The current still grows; only its rate slows.

questions.stem: The filament's resistance grows with current because:

options.text: the filament's temperature rises and its atoms vibrate more
options.explanation: Hotter lattice atoms obstruct the drifting electrons, raising the resistance.
No mass leaves the wire in normal operation.
The resistance rises rather than being destroyed.
Charge carriers are never manufactured by the current.

questions.stem: In reverse bias, a diode:

options.explanation: Large current belongs to forward bias.
Blocking is normal diode behaviour, not damage.
The reverse side of a diode graph is a flat zero region.

options.text: has a very high resistance and passes essentially no current
options.explanation: The reverse direction is the diode's blocked direction.

questions.stem: A diode conducts:

options.explanation: The whole point of a diode is its asymmetry.
Forward bias conducts freely.
Forward bias passes current; reverse bias blocks it.
Diode behaviour is about direction, not alternation.

questions.stem: Compared with a fixed resistor's graph, a filament lamp's graph:

options.explanation: The lamp's heating makes its graph bend.

options.text: bends as the resistance climbs with temperature
options.explanation: The curve records the growing resistance of the hot filament.
Current still grows with voltage; the slope stays positive.

options.text: never passes through the origin region at all
options.explanation: Both graphs start near zero and rise from there.

questions.stem: Describe the shape of a filament lamp's IV graph and state what happens to its resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: The graph curves so the current rises more slowly than the voltage; the lamp's resistance increases as the filament heats.

questions.stem: What is forward bias for a diode?
questions.modelAnswer: The direction in which the diode lets current flow — when the current lines up with the arrowhead of the symbol.

questions.stem: Explain why a diode passes no current in reverse bias.
questions.modelAnswer: In reverse bias the diode's resistance becomes extremely high, and a very large resistance chokes the current to effectively zero.

questions.stem: A diode is placed in a circuit backwards. State what the ammeter reads and what the IV graph shows on that side.
questions.modelAnswer: The ammeter reads zero, and the graph lies flat along the axis on the reverse side, showing the very high reverse resistance.

questions.stem: In the IV investigation, the independent variable is:

options.explanation: Voltage is the quantity read off — the dependent variable.

options.text: the current, adjusted with the variable resistor
options.explanation: The experimenter sets the current, making it independent.
The ammeter's resistance is assumed negligible and fixed.
Wire length is inside the variable resistor, not the measured variable.

questions.stem: The instrument that varies the current in the investigation is the:

options.explanation: The ammeter measures the current; it does not set it.
The voltmeter measures the voltage across the component.
Adjusting the variable resistor steps the current through the circuit.
The source provides the push; the resistor does the adjusting.

questions.stem: Increasing a circuit's resistance while the supply stays fixed makes the current:

options.explanation: More opposition at the same push means less flow.
That would need less resistance, not more.
Resistance is the dial that controls the current.
Direction of flow has nothing to do with the resistance size.

questions.stem: A variable resistor changes its resistance by:

options.explanation: Self-heating is the filament's story, not the variable resistor's control method.

options.text: altering the length of wire in the circuit
options.explanation: Sliding the contact changes how much wire the current must traverse.
Cells change the supply voltage, not the resistor.
Direction does not set a resistor's value.

questions.stem: A longer variable-resistor wire gives:

options.explanation: More wire means more opposition, not less.
The whole point of the slider is a changing resistance.
Wire never offers zero resistance in reality.
A longer wire carries more opposition for the charge to pass.

questions.stem: List the equipment needed to investigate how current varies with voltage.
questions.modelAnswer: An ammeter, a voltmeter, a variable resistor, a power source and connecting wires.

questions.stem: State which quantity is the independent variable in the IV investigation and which instrument changes it.
questions.modelAnswer: The current is independent, and the variable resistor is used to change it.

questions.stem: Explain why the voltmeter's readings form the dependent variable of the investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: The experimenter sets the current with the variable resistor and then reads off the voltage that results, so the voltage depends on the chosen current.

questions.stem: An investigator steps the current up five times, recording the voltage each time. What can be plotted from the pairs, and which shape signals a constant resistance?
questions.modelAnswer: The recorded pairs plot an IV graph; a straight line through the origin signals a constant resistance.
